nature-nbs-126.title: Africa's Great Green Wall: a belt of trees across the Sahel
nature-nbs-126.text: The plan was a wall of trees 15 km wide and 7,775 km long. The Great Green Wall is an African Union project adopted in 2007. It was first meant to stop desertification in the Sahel with a belt of trees from Djibouti to Senegal. It has since grown into a mosaic of green, productive landscapes using water harvesting and local land-use methods. By 2030 it aims to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land, capture 250 million tonnes of carbon dioxide and create 10 million jobs. Progress has been slow. A 2020 UNCCD report found only 4% of the planned area covered. In January 2021 partners pledged USD 14.3 billion, but by March 2023 only $2.5 billion had been paid out. As of 2024, about 30 million hectares had been restored, 30% of the target. Critics question its progress, funding and colonial framing, and some call for scrapping it. In 2023 it was said to face collapse from terrorism, weak leadership and too little funding.

nature-nbs-110.title: When new forests compete with farms and homes
nature-nbs-110.text: Government pledges to replant forests add up to 1.2bn hectares by 2060, a tenth of the world's land area. Reforestation can take land and water needed for food, grazing and housing, and may push out the people who use that land. Almost 300 million people live on land in the Global South identified as a tropical forest restoration opportunity. A WRI and IUCN map of 2 billion hectares for restoring forest is criticized for including 900 million hectares of grassland. Growing coffee under trees shows one way to blend forests with other uses.

nature-nbs-235.title: Sustainable agriculture: farming that can last
nature-nbs-235.text: Food systems cause one third of human greenhouse gas emissions. Agriculture's footprint is huge, and sustainable agriculture tries to shrink it. It is farming that reduces harm to the environment, maintains and builds up natural resources, and uses non-renewable resources productively. The aim is to produce crops or livestock without damaging soil, water, biodiversity, or the people on and near the farm. Its toolkit can include {{ref:nature-nbs-297}}, growing trees among crops, mixed farming, multiple cropping and rotating crops from season to season. In 1977 the USDA defined it as long-term practices that meet food needs and improve the environment. They should also use resources efficiently, keep farms viable and improve farmers' lives. Economics explains part of the problem. Environmental costs left out of a farmer's ordinary accounts are externalities, so the market does not punish them. Investment in sustainable farming is said to be four times more cost-effective than direct food aid. Yet it gets only three percent of humanitarian funds. Many certification systems exist, including organic labels, Rainforest Alliance and Fair Trade. People still disagree on what sustainability means here. An ecocentric view favors low growth and organic methods. A technocentric view relies on technology and modified industry.

nature-nbs-131.title: Rewilding: stepping back so nature can run itself
nature-nbs-131.text: In a Guyana forest, going from 5 to 35 mammal species raised the carbon in trees and soil four to five times. Results like that fuel interest in rewilding, a kind of ecological restoration that aims to raise biodiversity and restore natural processes while reducing human influence. Its key move is to replace human management with natural processes. Unlike other restoration, it accepts new mixes of species and interactions, the kind described in {{ref:nature-nbs-150}}. It often brings back large mammals to rebuild food webs, so that ecosystems regulate themselves. A group called Earth First coined the term in 1990. In 1998 Michael Soulé and Reed Noss gave it a scientific basis built on 'cores, corridors and carnivores': large reserves (see {{ref:nature-gov-038}}), links between them, and large predators. Supporters promote it as a natural climate solution through carbon storage, flood management and lower wildfire risk. It is also controversial. Critics question its evidence and its effect on farming and livelihoods.

nature-nbs-109.title: Paying people to plant forests or leave them standing
nature-nbs-109.text: A standing forest earns nothing for the person who could have cut it down. Financial incentives try to change that sum. They are payments, credits and tax breaks that reward landowners or countries for replanting forests or for not cutting them down. One proposal, 'compensated reduction', would pay developing countries that cut emissions from deforestation over an agreed period. Joining would be voluntary. But a country that signs up must cut emissions, and a missed target rolls into its next period. An emerging source of money is the sale of credits for carbon locked away in trees to companies and people offsetting their footprint. Such credits let farmers and private landowners earn money from replanting while gaining healthier soil. Governments also offer tax breaks to encourage companies to support reforestation.

nature-nbs-084.title: Forest monocultures: carbon gains, local losses
nature-nbs-084.text: In China, a shift to cheap plantings of mostly red pine meant trees died before delivering their expected carbon offset. Forest monocultures are plantations of a single tree species, often grown for timber. After deforestation, single-species afforestation has become popular as a way to lock away carbon. Eucalyptus, pines and acacias are common in the tropics and Global South, often imported species replacing native forest. Such schemes may help the global climate yet cause local harm, including soil depletion and altered water cycles. They reduce biodiversity and weaken resistance to pests and disease. They offer few local jobs, and profits follow a boom-and-bust pattern rarely reinvested in the land.

nature-nbs-145.title: Land restoration: returning land to a chosen state
nature-nbs-145.text: Restoring land starts with a choice: restore it to what? Land restoration, which may include rewilding, is returning land to a different or earlier state for a chosen purpose. The purposes vary. A project might make land safe, stabilize its ecological communities, clean up pollution, create a {{ref:nature-nbs-150}} or return land to a historical condition. Restoration answers damage caused mostly by people, such as pollution, deforestation, salination and species endangerment. It differs from land reclamation, which alters or destroys ecosystems to make way for farming or building. The payoff can be economic, because restored land can supply more valuable ecosystem services. Projects begin by surveying existing conditions. They then choose a reference ecosystem, a real or described system to measure success against. Increasingly, the mainstream approach uses Indigenous knowledge of the land, the subject of {{ref:nature-nbs-120}}, alongside Western science.

nature-nbs-122.title: Forest landscape restoration: planning for people and wildlife
nature-nbs-122.text: One restored hillside helps little if the valley around it keeps degrading. Forest landscape restoration (FLR) is a planned process to regain ecological integrity and improve human well-being across deforested or degraded landscapes. It links work at single sites to goals for a whole landscape, agreed among stakeholders. The concept grew out of work by the IUCN, WWF, the WRI and the International Tropical Timber Organization. It seeks compromises between the needs of people and wildlife, with local communities central to planning. Desired outcomes include tackling root causes of degradation, settling land-use conflicts, agreeing how benefits are shared and providing watershed services. A program can mix protecting secondary forest, {{ref:nature-nbs-138}}, planting framework trees, timber plantations and growing trees with crops. In 2014 FAO set up a mechanism to help countries meet the {{ref:nature-nbs-139}}.

nature-nbs-139.title: The Bonn Challenge: a global pledge to restore land
nature-nbs-139.text: On 2 September 2011, Germany and the IUCN launched a global goal in Bonn. The Bonn Challenge aims to restore 150 million hectares of degraded and deforested land by 2020 and 350 million hectares by 2030. The promised returns are large. The IUCN estimates meeting it would bring about $84 billion a year in net benefits, helping rural incomes. It is estimated to shrink the gap between planned and needed carbon dioxide cuts by 11-17%. Reaching 350 million hectares could bring up to $9 trillion in net benefits. Pakistan's Billion Tree Tsunami restored 350,000 hectares, beating its pledge. Not every pledge is what it seems, though. Nearly half were found to be land set aside for commercial wood use.

nature-nbs-120.title: Traditional ecological knowledge: restoration's long history
nature-nbs-120.text: Restoration is not a modern invention. {{ref:nature-gov-184}} have built up knowledge by observing and managing their environment, and it shows restoration practiced for thousands of years. These peoples shaped vegetation to meet their needs and sometimes increased populations and biodiversity. California Indians, for example, used concentrated forest burning. Because such knowledge is tied to place, restorers must take care not to appropriate it. Projects involving them should be led by them.

nature-nbs-101.title: The restoration economy: jobs from repairing nature
nature-nbs-101.text: In Oregon, every million invested in restoration created 15-24 jobs. That is the restoration economy at work: economic activity that comes from repairing land and nature. It is set against activity built on sprawl or on using up natural resources. The idea is that repairing past damage often pays off at local, regional and national scales. The phrase spread after Storm Cunningham's 2002 book The Restoration Economy, which sorted restorative development into eight sectors. Four focus on nature: ecological, watershed and fishery restoration, plus {{ref:nature-nbs-258}}. Projects need workers, materials and services, so spending creates local jobs and business. The Oregon study found each dollar generated another 1.4 to 2.4 dollars, with effects similar to road building. The jobs have a downside. Hand work such as planting trees pays less than logging, is less reliable, and is mostly done by immigrant workers.

nature-nbs-226.title: Carbon farming: pulling carbon from the air into soil
nature-nbs-226.text: Turning a forest, grassland or savanna into cropland cuts the soil's organic carbon by about 30–40%. Carbon farming tries to run that process in reverse. It is a set of farming and forestry methods meant to store carbon from the air in soil and living plants. The overall goal is a net removal of carbon from the atmosphere, by speeding up how fast carbon is locked away. Methods include changing tillage and grazing, using mulch or compost, adding {{ref:nature-clim-178}} and changing which crops are grown. This charcoal, mixed into soil, locks away roughly 50% of the carbon in the original biomass. The potential is large. Carbon farming could offset as much as 20% of 2010 carbon dioxide emissions each year, and by 2016 its variants covered hundreds of millions of hectares. Farmers who store carbon can sell credits to companies that need offsets, as in Australia. But the storage is not permanent. Disturbing the soil or tilling hard turns it back into a source of greenhouse gases. If incentives reward only stored carbon, they could encourage land clearing, single-crop farming and biodiversity loss. The effect on crop yields is unsettled, and critics doubt the practices can spread widely enough to matter.

nature-nbs-276.title: Crop rotation: changing what grows, season by season
nature-nbs-276.text: Plant the same crop year after year and the soil tires of it. Growing one crop repeatedly, called monocropping, drains particular nutrients and breeds specialized pests. Crop rotation is the fix: growing a sequence of different crops on the same land over successive seasons. It stops crops drawing on one set of nutrients and reduces pests, weeds and resistance. Changing crops interrupts pest life cycles and habitat. Rotating nitrogen-fixing legumes such as clover with nitrogen-hungry crops supplies nitrogen to the crops that follow. Rotations, especially diverse long ones, greatly increase soil organic carbon. Different crops also spread the farmer's risk from bad weather. During the Green Revolution, developed countries largely replaced rotation with chemical fertilizers. Today US rules for certified organic farms require it.

nature-nbs-258.title: Regenerative agriculture: farming to rebuild, not just sustain
nature-nbs-258.text: An estimated 30–75% of global soil organic matter has been lost since tillage-based farming began. Regenerative agriculture aims to win some of it back. It seeks to restore rather than just sustain, rebuilding topsoil, biodiversity and ecosystem services. It is not one practice but a mix of sustainable techniques, such as reusing farm waste and adding compost. The Rodale Institute began using the term in the early 1980s. A 2020 review of 229 articles and 25 websites found no legal or broadly accepted definition. Its four most consistent principles are improving soil health, optimizing resource use, easing climate change and improving water. A 2023 review found practices like reduced tillage and growing trees on farms can help soil carbon or yields in some conditions, but evidence is limited. Some scientists call the climate claims, especially for grazing, exaggerated.

nature-nbs-246.title: Agroecology: ecology applied to the farm
nature-nbs-246.text: Organics is practiced in 188 countries, and it is one of three certified forms of agroecology. Agroecology is the study and practice of applying ecological processes to farming, looking at links between plants, animals, people and the environment. The term can mean a science, a set of practices, or a social movement. It draws on agronomy, ecology, sociology, economics and history. It studies farm ecosystems' productivity, stability, sustainability and fairness, at scales from a gene to the globe. Unlike in natural ecology, human activity and economics are the main forces at work. Biodynamic farming, organics and China's Green Food are its certified varieties. Movements such as La Via Campesina use it to pursue food sovereignty. Researchers heatedly debate which model of farming policy should support.

nature-nbs-233.title: Landscape-scale conservation: managing the whole picture
nature-nbs-233.text: A river basin supplies water, timber, crops and habitat, and each use affects the others. Landscape-scale conservation manages the whole landscape to balance nature against farming, forestry and other uses of the same land. It is an alternative to protecting single sites. Its backers argue that {{ref:nature-gov-005}}, food security, climate change, water scarcity and biodiversity loss are linked and need coordinated action. Rather than serve one land use, it tries to meet many stakeholders' interests. The IUCN applied it in 27 landscapes in 23 countries. In 2015 UNEP described this landscape approach as managing whole ecosystems rather than single resources. A review found five barriers, including confusing terms, long delays before action and sectors working in silos.

nature-nbs-260.title: Riparian buffers: green strips that guard streams
nature-nbs-260.text: A nine-year University of Georgia study found streamside buffers removed at least 60% of nitrogen and 65% of phosphorus from fertilizer washing off fields. A riparian buffer is a strip of vegetation, usually trees, along a stream that shades it and shields it from nearby land use. Buffers catch sediment, nutrients and pesticides before they reach the water. They counter eutrophication downstream and stabilize banks. They also provide habitat and wildlife corridors in farm country. Buffers can raise land value and grow profitable crops such as black walnut and hazelnut. Programs such as the US Conservation Reserve Program pay farmers for the land taken out of production. They have limits: a 2017 study found little ability to stop glyphosate leaching to streams.

nature-nbs-231.title: Scoring how well farms can weather climate change
nature-nbs-231.text: How ready is a country's farming for a hotter, less predictable climate? The Climate-Resilient Agriculture Index tries to put a number on it. The global version benchmarks countries with nine indicators in three dimensions: productivity and efficient use of resources, environmental sustainability and climate impact, and socio-economic resilience. It sorts nations into four levels, from Highly Resilient to Very Low Resilience. A version for India uses 26 indicators to compare its agro-climatic zones.

nature-nbs-230.title: Climate-smart farming that works for women
nature-nbs-230.text: Women farmers in developing countries face more danger from climate change than men. They have less access to land, money and advice. They are also often left out of decisions, which can limit their use of practices that help them adapt. Gender-responsive climate-smart agriculture designs programs around the different constraints and abilities of women and men farmers.

nature-nbs-265.title: Regenerative economics: renewing Earth's capital
nature-nbs-265.text: Regenerative economics treats the Earth as the original capital asset, to be renewed rather than used up. In standard theory an asset can be regenerated or consumed until it yields nothing more. Supporters say ignoring nature's value has caused {{ref:nature-eecon-090}}, a term coined by {{ref:nature-hist-040}}. The approach has four components: circulation, organizational structure, relationships and values, and collective learning. {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} sets limits on the economy, while this approach focuses on renewing life in nature.

nature-nbs-075.title: Greenwashing: selling a green image instead of green action
nature-nbs-075.text: In 1986 New York environmentalist Jay Westerveld noticed hotels urging guests to reuse towels to 'save the environment'. The main effect was lower laundry costs. His essay coined a word blending 'green' with 'whitewashing'. Greenwashing is advertising or public relations meant to mislead people into believing an organization's products, goals or policies are good for the environment. Firms do it to win legitimacy with environmentally minded people, to look responsible to the wider public, and to distance themselves from their own or their suppliers' failings. A common rule of thumb: an organization is greenwashing if it spends far more on advertising a green image than on acting in environmentally sound ways. The practice is widespread. A 2020 European Union study found over 50% of examined environmental claims were vague, misleading or unfounded, and 40% were unsubstantiated. Many companies pledged to reach net zero, balancing emissions with removals, after the 2015 {{ref:nature-clim-074}}, but critics say their plans are unfeasible rather than real cuts. With no agreed definition, consumers and regulators can struggle to call a case. Critics argue that widespread greenwashing, with weak enforcement, makes consumers doubt all green claims. That weakens their power to push firms toward greener practices.

nature-nbs-082.title: Monoculture: one crop, one field, short-term gains
nature-nbs-082.text: Over 600 million liters of pesticides are sprayed each year after pest outbreaks. Many of those outbreaks trace back to monoculture, growing a single crop species in a field at a time. In the short term it is easy and efficient: uniform planting, care and harvest often give higher yields and lower costs. With synthetic fertilizers, it has reduced the extra land needed for food, which is called land sparing. Over the long term, though, monocultures are more prone to disease and pests, because local biodiversity falls and nutrients run down. Perennial monocultures such as oil palm, sugarcane, tea and pines can acidify and degrade soils. Declining soil health leads to more fertilizer, whose excess nitrogen can contaminate drinking water and feed algal blooms. Diversity can be added through crop rotation, intercropping, agroecology, silvopasture and {{ref:nature-nbs-086}}.

nature-nbs-088.title: Planting trees to fight climate change: promise and limits
nature-nbs-088.text: Forests take up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year. Using new trees to pull carbon dioxide from the air and store it is an obvious idea for limiting climate change. Forests can switch roles, though. In 2019 they absorbed a third less carbon than in the 1990s, because of heat, drought and deforestation. Avoiding deforestation beats clearing and replanting. Clearing causes irreversible biodiversity loss and soil damage, and new forests take several decades to deliver comparable carbon benefits. Scientists call protecting and restoring carbon-rich, long-lived ecosystems, especially natural forests, 'the major climate solution'. One estimate found room for 0.9 billion ha more tree canopy, and it has been criticized as far too high. Counting albedo and other feedbacks, the area that truly cools is 20-80% lower. That planting would store 205 billion tons of carbon only if the trees survive future climate stress to maturity. The carbon must also not return to the air when trees burn or rot. Plantations mixing several species would store more than single-species ones.

nature-nbs-080.title: Bluewashing: greenwashing for the oceans
nature-nbs-080.text: Bluewashing is a term closely akin to greenwashing. It means false or misleading claims about how an action affects water and ocean environments. The term comes up in discussions of the blue economy, the lasting, careful development of coastal and ocean resources.
